text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests that measure your blood glucose or average blood sugar levels over time.
snippet_highlighted_words: using specific blood tests that measure your blood glucose or average blood sugar levels over time

text_blocks.snippet: According to guidelines from the American Diabetes Association, type 2 diabetes is diagnosed if you meet any of the following thresholds:

list.snippet: Hemoglobin A1C Test: 6.5% or higher (measures average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months).
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or higher (taken after fasting with no caloric intake for at least 8 hours).
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher (measured 2 hours after drinking a 75-gram glucose solution).
Random Plasma Glucose Test: 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher in someone who is having classic symptoms of high blood sugar (such as frequent urination, extreme thirst, or unexplained weight loss).

Repeat Testing: If you do not have classic, severe symptoms of high blood sugar, doctors usually require a second abnormal test result (either repeating the same test or using a different test) to confirm the diagnosis.

Prediabetes Range: If your numbers fall between normal and diabetic levels, you may be diagnosed with prediabetes (A1C of 5.7%–6.4%, fasting glucose of 100–125 mg/dL, or 2-hour OGTT of 140–199 mg/dL).

text_blocks.snippet: Learn more about blood sugar ranges and preparation guidelines on MedlinePlus.
